name: Clobazam (Onfi, Sympazan)
summary: Long-acting benzodiazepine mainly used to treat certain hard-to-control seizures (like Lennox–Gastaut syndrome). Very sedating, habit-forming, and especially dangerous when combined with opioids or alcohol.
description: Clobazam is a long-acting benzodiazepine that helps calm overactive brain activity, mainly used as an add-on treatment for seizures in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome. It can also be used off-label for other seizure types and, less commonly, short-term for severe anxiety. Because it is a benzodiazepine, it carries serious risks: sleepiness, slowed breathing (especially with opioids), dependence, and withdrawal if stopped too quickly. It should be used at the lowest effective dose, for as short a time as possible, with careful monitoring.
patient_summary: Clobazam is usually prescribed for certain hard-to-treat seizures, especially in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome. It’s a benzodiazepine, similar in family to medications like Valium, but designed mainly for seizures. It can help reduce seizure frequency, but it also makes many people sleepy or groggy. Over time, your body can get used to it (dependence), so you should never stop it suddenly—doses must be reduced slowly under medical supervision. Mixing clobazam with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives can be extremely dangerous and lead to slowed or stopped breathing.

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved as an add-on (adjunctive) medication to reduce seizures in patients ≥2 years old with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.
Used off-label to help control seizures in Dravet syndrome when other antiseizure medications are not enough.
Often added when seizures remain uncontrolled despite multiple antiseizure drugs.
Sometimes used only around the menstrual period to reduce seizure flares.
Can be used short-term for severe anxiety when other treatments are not yet working, but not a first-line anxiety medication because of dependence and withdrawal risks.

contraindications: Known allergy or serious reaction to clobazam or any ingredient in the product
Current serious respiratory compromise (e.g., severe COPD, significant sleep apnea) without close monitoring
History of benzodiazepine abuse or significant substance use disorder (strong relative contraindication)
Concurrent use with opioids unless there is no alternative and close monitoring is in place

efficacy_response.percentage_value: Many patients achieve clinically meaningful seizure reduction
efficacy_response.comparison_data: In clinical trials, clobazam led to significant reductions in drop seizures compared with placebo when added to existing antiseizure medications.
efficacy_response.patient_text: Clobazam usually doesn’t stop seizures completely by itself, but it can meaningfully reduce how often and how severe they are when added to a seizure regimen—especially in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: Pivotal Onfi trials – LGS adjunctive therapy

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Rapid and extensive after oral dosing; not significantly affected by food.
pharmacokinetics.onset: Seizure benefit builds over several days; maximal effect often seen within 1–2 weeks as steady-state is reached.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Clobazam: ~36–42 hours; active metabolite N-desmethylclobazam: ~71–82 hours (very long-acting).
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Classified as long-acting due to long half-life and active metabolite.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Processed in the liver mainly by CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 to an active metabolite; CYP2C19 poor metabolizers have much higher levels.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Eliminated mostly in urine as metabolites; small amount in stool.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food and tablet crushing do not meaningfully alter overall absorption.

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: Clobazam is mainly an epilepsy medication, not a general anti-anxiety pill, even though it belongs to the benzodiazepine family.
items: {link:condition:lennox-gastaut-syndrome:Lennox–Gastaut Syndrome}: Add-on therapy to reduce seizures in children and adults ≥2 years
{link:condition:epilepsy-refractory-seizures:Refractory (hard-to-control) seizures}: Often added when other antiseizure drugs are not enough
{link:condition:dravet-syndrome:Dravet Syndrome}: Used off-label in treatment plans designed by epilepsy specialists
{link:condition:catamenial-epilepsy:Catamenial Epilepsy}: Short courses around the menstrual period to lessen seizure flares
off_label: Short-term treatment of severe anxiety when other options are not yet effective (often only for a few weeks)
Other treatment-resistant generalized or focal seizures as part of an individualized epilepsy plan

sections.heading: What People Often Notice
sections.intro: Experiences vary, but many people and caregivers describe a mix of seizure benefits and sedation-related side effects.

quotes: We noticed fewer and shorter seizures after a week or two.
The drop seizures decreased a lot, even though they didn’t disappear completely.
Her ‘big’ seizures still happen, but not as often or as severe.
He’s more sleepy and less interactive during the day.
I feel like I’m in a fog—slower to think and respond.
We had to adjust the dose because she was too drowsy in school.
items.note: Sleepiness, slowed thinking, and drooling are common, especially at higher doses.

quotes: Sometimes he seems more irritable and aggressive.
Her mood swings got worse when the dose went up.
We had to watch closely for changes in behavior.
items.note: Paradoxical reactions (agitation, aggression) can occur, especially in children and older adults.

quotes: When we tried to lower it too fast, the seizures got much worse.
Missing doses made me feel shaky and anxious.
We had to taper really slowly to avoid withdrawal symptoms.
items.note: Clobazam can cause physical dependence; doses must be reduced gradually to avoid withdrawal and seizure worsening.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Clobazam is not a fast “rescue” medication—it is a maintenance medicine that builds up over days.
key_points: First few days: Sedation and drowsiness are often noticed before seizure benefits.
5–9 days: Maximum antiseizure effect typically becomes more evident.
Long-acting: Both clobazam and its active metabolite stay in the body for many days.
Once or twice daily: Most dosing plans use 1–2 doses per day, depending on total daily dose.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Combining benzodiazepines like clobazam with opioids can be fatal.
sections.black_box: Using clobazam together with opioids (such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, morphine, or fentanyl) can cause extreme sleepiness, dangerously slowed breathing, coma, and death. These medicines should only be used together when no safer alternatives exist, at the lowest effective doses, and with close medical supervision.
other: Abuse, misuse, and addiction: Clobazam is a benzodiazepine and a controlled substance. It can be misused and is habit-forming. Taking more than prescribed, using it for non-medical reasons, or combining it with alcohol/other drugs greatly increases the risk of overdose and death.

Dependence and withdrawal: The body adapts to clobazam over time. Stopping suddenly or lowering the dose too quickly can trigger withdrawal symptoms (anxiety, tremors, agitation, seizures), which can be life-threatening.
Respiratory depression: Clobazam can slow breathing, especially in people with lung disease, sleep apnea, or those using other sedatives.

Serious skin reactions: Rare but severe skin reactions (Stevens–Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis) can occur, usually in the first 8 weeks. Any new, widespread, or blistering rash needs urgent medical attention.

Multiorgan hypersensitivity: Fever, rash, swollen glands, and problems with liver, kidneys, or blood cells can occur as a severe allergic-type reaction. This requires immediate discontinuation and medical care.

Suicidal thoughts and behavior: Like other antiseizure medications, clobazam may slightly increase the risk of suicidal thoughts or actions. Monitor for new or worsening mood changes, irritability, or self-harm thoughts.
Paradoxical reactions: In some people, especially children and older adults, clobazam can cause increased agitation, aggression, or disinhibition instead of calming effects.
Older adults: Higher risks of falls, confusion, breathing problems, and death. Use only when clearly needed and at the lowest effective dose.
patient_counseling: Never mix clobazam with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives unless your doctor has specifically instructed you and is monitoring you closely.
Do not increase your dose, take extra doses, or use someone else’s clobazam. This is dangerous and illegal.
Never stop clobazam suddenly. Work with your specialist on a slow taper plan if it needs to be reduced or stopped.
Call your doctor right away if you notice new or worsening depression, mood changes, aggression, or suicidal thoughts.
Seek urgent care if you develop a painful or blistering skin rash, trouble breathing, severe sleepiness, or signs of allergic reactions (swelling of the face, lips, tongue).
If you have a history of substance use problems, tell your provider before starting clobazam so you can be monitored more closely.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Sleepiness, drooling, and behavior changes are common. Serious breathing problems, severe rash, and withdrawal reactions are less common but can be life-threatening.

common.incidence: Very common (up to ~25% or more, dose-related)
common.patient_note: Expect increased sleepiness, especially when starting or increasing the dose. Avoid driving or risky activities until you know how clobazam affects you.
Extra saliva and drooling are frequently reported, especially in children. Talk with your provider if this affects comfort, swallowing, or skin around the mouth.
Some patients become more agitated or aggressive instead of calmer. Caregivers should watch closely and report behavior changes promptly.
Use caution with stairs and uneven surfaces. This side effect increases fall risk, especially in older adults.
Nausea, vomiting, and changes in appetite can occur. Hydration, fiber, and meal timing adjustments may help; tell your provider if severe or persistent.
Upper respiratory infections and pneumonia have been reported more frequently in patients taking clobazam, especially those with neurologic disabilities.

serious: Severe allergic reactions: swelling of face/lips/tongue, trouble breathing, or widespread rash.
Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis: painful rash, blisters, skin peeling, sores in mouth or eyes—medical emergency.
Severe respiratory depression: very slow or shallow breathing, blue lips, confusion, difficult to wake—especially when combined with opioids or alcohol.
Suicidal thoughts or behavior: new or sudden changes in mood, self-harm thoughts, or unusual agitation.
Multiorgan hypersensitivity: fever, swollen glands, rash, and problems with liver, kidney, blood, or other organs.
Withdrawal seizures and severe withdrawal symptoms if stopped abruptly or tapered too quickly.

sections.heading: Drug and Substance Interactions
sections.intro: Clobazam interacts with many medications and substances, especially other sedatives and certain antiseizure drugs.

items.risk: Profound sedation, severe respiratory depression, coma, and death.
items.action: Avoid combination when possible. If absolutely necessary, use the lowest effective doses with close monitoring and consider having naloxone on hand.

items.with: Alcohol and other sedatives (benzodiazepines, sleep medications, barbiturates, many muscle relaxants)
items.risk: Additive or synergistic sedation and breathing suppression; high risk of overdose and accidents.
items.action: Avoid or minimize. Do not drink alcohol while on clobazam without direct medical guidance.

items.risk: May change clobazam or other drug levels; can increase sedation or alter seizure control.
items.action: Your neurologist will adjust doses and may monitor blood levels for complex regimens.

items.with: Strong CYP2C19 inhibitors (e.g., some heartburn and antifungal medications)
items.risk: Higher levels of the active metabolite, leading to more sedation and side effects.
items.action: Dose reductions and slower titration may be needed; your provider may order drug levels in some cases.

items.with: Medications that depress breathing (e.g., some anesthetics, high-dose gabapentinoids)
items.risk: Increased risk of respiratory depression and hospitalization.
items.action: Use with great caution and under specialist supervision.

sections.heading: Stopping Clobazam Safely
sections.text: Because clobazam is a long-acting benzodiazepine, stopping too quickly can be dangerous and may cause severe withdrawal, including seizures.
key_points: Never stop clobazam suddenly after regular use. This can trigger withdrawal seizures and other serious symptoms.
For short-term, lower-dose use without misuse: doses are often reduced by 20–25% each week, adjusting based on symptoms.
For long-term, high-dose use or suspected benzodiazepine use disorder: tapers may reduce the dose by about 25% every 1–2 weeks at first, then slow down as doses get smaller.
Some people, especially on high doses for a long time, may need several months to taper safely.
If severe anxiety, agitation, or seizures appear during a taper, the plan may need to pause or be slowed under medical supervision.

sections.heading: Dosing Information (Adults)
sections.text: Clobazam dosing depends on the condition being treated, age, weight, and other medical issues. Epilepsy specialists usually guide dosing and changes.

adult.lgs_initial: 5 mg twice daily for at least 1 week.
adult.lgs_titration: Increase to 10 mg twice daily for ≥1 week, then to 20 mg twice daily if needed based on response and side effects.
adult.lgs_max: Typically 40 mg/day for most adults; some refractory cases may go higher under expert supervision.
adult.anxiety_off_label: Common off-label ranges: 20–30 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses, with gradual titration up to 80 mg/day in select cases. Use short-term and only when other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated.
adult.refractory_seizures_off_label: Often starts at 5–15 mg/day, titrated slowly up to 40 mg/day; in some cases up to 80 mg/day under close specialist oversight.
adult.cyp2c19_poor_metabolizers: Start at lowest doses (e.g., 5 mg once daily) and titrate much more slowly; usual maximum is about half the normal max, with further increases delayed until at least 3 weeks after starting.
adult.hepatic_impairment_mild_to_moderate: Initial 5 mg once daily for ≥1 week; then 5 mg twice daily; then 10 mg twice daily; may increase to 20 mg twice daily if tolerated (max 40 mg/day).
adult.elderly: Start at lower doses (e.g., 5 mg once daily), titrate cautiously, and rarely exceed 40 mg/day due to increased sensitivity and slower clearance.

sections.simple_explanation: Doses are increased slowly over weeks to balance seizure control against side effects like sleepiness and behavior changes. Because clobazam stays in the body for a long time, changes should not be rushed.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Clobazam can be important for seizure control, but it also carries risks during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Decisions should be made with specialists.
sections.pregnancy: All antiseizure drugs, including clobazam, must be weighed carefully in pregnancy. Uncontrolled seizures are dangerous for both parent and baby, but benzodiazepines can cause birth defects in some studies, and late pregnancy use may lead to newborn sedation or withdrawal. If a patient becomes pregnant while taking clobazam, do not stop suddenly; contact neurology and obstetrics to plan the safest approach. Folic acid supplementation and enrollment in antiseizure pregnancy registries are recommended.
sections.lactation: Clobazam and its active metabolite pass into breast milk. Some breastfed infants may become sleepy or have feeding or weight-gain issues. If clobazam is used while breastfeeding, the infant should be monitored for sedation, poor feeding, and poor weight gain. In some cases, a shorter-acting benzodiazepine may be preferred for anxiety treatment during breastfeeding, but clobazam may still be appropriate for seizure control under specialist care.
sections.pediatrics: Approved as adjunctive therapy for Lennox–Gastaut syndrome in children ≥2 years. Doses are weight-based and titrated slowly. Children are particularly prone to sedation, drooling, and behavior changes; careful monitoring by caretakers and specialists is essential.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults clear clobazam more slowly and are more sensitive to sedative effects, falls, confusion, and breathing problems. Lower starting doses, slower titration, and strict maximum doses are critical. Beers Criteria list benzodiazepines as potentially inappropriate in most older adults except in specific cases (e.g., seizure disorders).
sections.hepatic: Because clobazam is extensively metabolized in the liver, people with liver impairment need lower initial doses, slower titration, and lower maximum doses. Severe liver disease requires extreme caution or alternative options.
sections.renal: Mild to moderate kidney impairment usually does not need dose changes, but severe impairment has not been well studied—careful monitoring is needed.

sections.heading: What Clinicians Monitor
items: Seizure frequency, severity, and type: to assess benefit.
Level of sedation, cognition, and coordination: risk of falls and accidents.
Breathing: especially if there is lung disease, sleep apnea, or concurrent opioid use.
Mood and behavior: agitation, aggression, depression, or suicidal thoughts.
Skin: early signs of rash or blistering suggesting SJS/TEN.
Signs of abuse or misuse: early refills, escalating doses, taking more than prescribed, doctor shopping.
Withdrawal symptoms: during dose reductions or if doses are missed.
Liver function and blood counts: if clinically indicated or if symptoms suggest organ problems.
Drug levels (clobazam and N-desmethylclobazam): in complex cases, pregnancy, or suspected toxicity, as guided by epilepsy specialists.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Multiple formulations are available to accommodate different ages and swallowing abilities.
items: Tablets (Onfi and generics): 10 mg and 20 mg (scored; can be split or crushed and mixed with soft food like applesauce).
Oral suspension: 2.5 mg/mL (must be shaken well; use the provided dosing syringe).
Oral film (Sympazan): 5 mg, 10 mg, and 20 mg films placed on top of the tongue to dissolve (do not chew; do not take more than one film at a time).

sections.heading: How It Works in the Brain
sections.text: Clobazam is a 1,5-benzodiazepine that attaches to specific sites on the GABA-A receptor, the brain’s main “brake” system. By enhancing GABA’s calming effect, it helps quiet overactive nerve activity and reduce seizures. Because of its long half-life and active metabolite, its calming and antiseizure effects last a long time—but so do its sedating and dependence effects.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment
sections.text: Clobazam is usually not a first-line treatment for epilepsy in general, but it is a key option for Lennox–Gastaut syndrome and some treatment-resistant epilepsies. It is added on top of other antiseizure drugs when seizures remain uncontrolled. As an anxiety treatment, clobazam is rarely a first choice—safer and less addictive options (like SSRIs, SNRIs, and therapy) are preferred. Because of dependence, withdrawal, and breathing risks, long-term use is reserved for carefully selected patients under specialist care.

seo.title: Clobazam (Onfi, Sympazan): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects & Safety
seo.description: Clobazam for Lennox–Gastaut syndrome and refractory seizures: how it works, dosing, serious risks with opioids, dependence and withdrawal, side effects, pregnancy/breastfeeding, and safe tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed for accuracy against current FDA labeling, epilepsy treatment guidelines, and up-to-date literature on benzodiazepine safety, dependence, and use in special populations.

faqs.a: Clobazam is mainly used as an add-on medication to reduce seizures in people with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (LGS) who are 2 years or older. It’s also used off-label for other hard-to-control seizures and, less commonly, short-term for severe anxiety when safer options are not yet working.

faqs.q: Is clobazam the same as other benzodiazepines like Xanax or Valium?
faqs.a: Clobazam is in the same family (benzodiazepines), but it is designed primarily as an antiseizure medication. Like Xanax or Valium, it can cause sedation, dependence, and withdrawal, but its main role is seizure control rather than day-to-day anxiety treatment.

faqs.q: How long does clobazam take to work for seizures?
faqs.a: Clobazam doesn’t work instantly. It builds up over several days. Many people see seizure improvement within 1–2 weeks as the dose is slowly increased and steady levels are reached.

Yes, clobazam is often used long-term for seizure disorders when it clearly helps and the benefits outweigh the risks. However, because of dependence, tolerance, and side effects (especially sedation and breathing risks), it should be regularly reviewed by your specialist to confirm it’s still needed.

Clobazam is a benzodiazepine and a Schedule IV controlled substance, which means it can be habit-forming. Your body can become physically dependent, and misuse can lead to addiction. Taking more than prescribed or combining it with alcohol or other drugs increases the risk of overdose and death.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on clobazam?
faqs.a: It’s strongly discouraged. Alcohol adds to clobazam’s sedative effects and can severely slow your breathing, especially if you’re also taking other sedatives or opioids. This combination can be life-threatening.

faqs.q: What happens if I stop clobazam suddenly?
faqs.a: Stopping clobazam abruptly can cause dangerous withdrawal symptoms, including severe anxiety, tremors, and seizures (sometimes worse than before treatment). Never stop it suddenly—always work with your neurologist to slowly taper the dose.

There are potential risks to the fetus with benzodiazepines, but uncontrolled seizures are also dangerous. If you become pregnant while on clobazam, do not stop it on your own. Contact your neurologist and obstetric provider right away to weigh benefits and risks and to plan the safest course of action.

faqs.q: Can I breastfeed while taking clobazam?
faqs.a: Clobazam and its active metabolite pass into breast milk. Some infants may become very sleepy or have trouble feeding or gaining weight. Your healthcare team can help you decide whether to continue clobazam, adjust doses, or consider alternatives, and will monitor your baby closely if you breastfeed.

faqs.q: What are signs that the dose may be too high?
faqs.a: Warning signs include extreme sleepiness, confusion, difficulty waking, very slow or shallow breathing, severe drooling, marked behavior changes (aggression or agitation), or frequent falls. These symptoms need urgent medical review.
